analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Sarbanes-Oxley rule requiring companies to certify their internal financial controls.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2005 with a single cosponsor and never received a committee vote; it died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, the post-Enron rule that requires public companies to assess their internal controls against accounting fraud and requires an outside auditor to verify that assessment [S2][S3]. It would also erase the accountability framework tied to those certifications [S2][S3]. The bill never advanced past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Executives and directors of public companies, who would no longer have to formally assess and certify their internal financial controls, and would shed the compliance costs and accountability that come with that requirement [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the requirement that management state its responsibility for internal controls and assess their effectiveness in each annual report [S2][S3].
Eliminates the requirement that an outside audit firm attest to and report on management's internal-control assessment [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Investors, who would lose the assurance that a company's financial statements rest on checked internal controls — the safeguard adopted after accounting scandals at Enron and WorldCom.

drawbacks.text: Removing the internal-control assessment and audit attestation would leave investors with less independent verification that a company's books are reliable [S2][S3].

The strongest good-faith objection to the rule is that Section 404 compliance carried real costs, which fell hardest on smaller public companies; this bill would have removed that burden but also the investor protection it funded.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — lower compliance costs for public companies, especially smaller ones — is real but narrow, and it comes by stripping out the main investor-protection safeguard enacted after the Enron-era accounting scandals. The cost falls on ordinary shareholders and retirement savers, who would have less assurance that corporate financial reports are trustworthy. On balance, the bill serves management more than the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to a subcommittee, and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Paul introduced the bill on April 14, 2005, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1][S5].
On May 19, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Capital Markets, Insurance and Government Sponsored Enterprises, where it stayed [S5].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor and received no committee markups, floor votes, or further action before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Investors and retirement savers are better off, because the rollback of the internal-control requirements never advanced. Public-company managements avoided nothing, since the Sarbanes-Oxley rules they sought to repeal stayed on the books.

for.name: Rep. Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal Sarbanes-Oxley's internal-control certification requirements and made introductory remarks on it.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote; it was sent to a subcommittee and sat there for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested; the bill's only recorded support was its Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor [S4].

industries.note: Repeal would free management from formally assessing and certifying internal financial controls, cutting their compliance burden and exposure if reporting goes wrong. The assurance those certifications give investors is the cost.

Repeal would eliminate the mandated Section 404 attestation work, a significant revenue stream for large audit firms, while also ending the liability that comes with vouching for management's assessments. Investors lose the outside check the attestation provides.
